dashboard.source: next-app/src/lib/providers.ts: PROVIDERS, CATALOG_ALIAS and Supabase tokenHowTo

notes: Indexed object types and setup notes are from public ProviderInfoFor output, not dashboard marketing summaries.
Supabase has no normalizer provider description; push-only behavior and setup are sourced from the dashboard provider tokenHowTo.
An empty indexed_object_types list is preserved and does not imply that no content syncs.

providers.name: PagerDuty
setup_guide: Create a READ-ONLY REST API key: PagerDuty → Integrations → API Access Keys → Create New API Key, and tick Read-only. This connector never writes, and a full-access key would let a leaked token trigger or resolve real incidents.

Set the email field to the account the key belongs to. PagerDuty sends it as the From header and rejects calls where it does not match a real user, so a mistyped address fails every request rather than some of them.

Mint the key at the ACCOUNT level, not scoped to a single user. A user-scoped key cannot list services, so discovery returns nothing and there is no way to choose what to sync — an empty picker is what that mistake looks like.

Services are picked after connecting. Incidents are scoped to the services you select, including their alerts, notes and status updates; schedules and escalation policies are account-wide and always synced, which is what makes "who is on call" answerable.

Incident notes and status updates are indexed by default because they are where the human response text lives. Turn off fetch_incident_prose if you would rather not index them, or to cut the per-incident request count on a very large account. Disabling excludes the note text; the fact that a note was added stays visible in the incident timeline.

With permission-aware search on, each service is readable by PagerDuty owners and admins, and by everyone else only from inside one of its teams (a service on no team is readable by every role that reads public services). Schedules and escalation policies carry the same rule over their own teams and are refreshed every sync. PagerDuty's API does not say whether a team is private, so a Manager, Responder or Observer outside a team does not see its services here even when the team is public. The read-only key must be able to read users, teams, services, schedules and escalation policies; when it cannot, the service is readable by everyone in your workspace, with a warning on the connector, until you reconnect or set an access rule on it.

providers.name: Datadog
setup_guide: Datadog needs TWO keys and they do different jobs. Create an API key under Organization Settings → API Keys, and an application key under Organization Settings → Application Keys. The API key identifies the org; the application key carries the scopes, so it is the one that decides what syncs.

An application key is created UNSCOPED and the create dialog has no scope picker — the key list will show it as "Not Scoped", meaning it inherits everything its owner can do. You have to open the key afterwards and Edit it to apply scopes, so a key made the obvious way is a full-permission key.

Grant exactly these and nothing more: timeseries_query, slos_read, logs_read_data, monitors_read, dashboards_read, notebooks_read and incident_read. Datadog's own description of logs_read_data claims reading logs also needs "Logs Read Index Data"; tested against a live org it does not, so do not grant the extra one.

A missing scope does not fail loudly. Datadog answers an unauthorized request with a bare 403 that names no permission, an unknown metric with a 200 and an empty series, and a log query against an org with no indexes with "No valid indexes specified" — so an under-scoped key looks exactly like an empty account.
Both keys are site-specific. If your org is not on US1, set the site field (for example us5.datadoghq.com or datadoghq.eu) or every call fails against the wrong region.

Datadog has nothing to browse, so the resource step offers a single "All data" row — select it to continue. It syncs the whole org: monitors are indexed with their message text, which is where runbooks live, along with dashboards, SLO definitions, notebooks and declared incidents.

Incidents Datadog marks PRIVATE are indexed too, and their restriction is carried over: Datadog scopes a private incident to its participants, and we record it as visible to nobody, so an access-scoped search never returns it. Each indexed incident also records its own visibility in its text, so you can tell which is which.

That mirroring only takes effect once access-scoped search is enabled for this connector on our side, which is a per-provider setting rather than something the scopes control. Until it is on, a private incident behaves the way it did before and is searchable by everyone in your HydraDB tenant. Ask us to turn it on, or skip just the incident_read scope if that trade is not acceptable: every other stream syncs without it.

The metric query, log query and SLO id fields are optional additions, each selecting one extra time series to index. Leaving them blank costs you those series and nothing else — everything above syncs without them.

providers.name: Asana
setup_guide: Create a personal access token in Asana's Developer Console under My apps → Personal access tokens. PATs inherit the creating user's visibility and have no scope picker, so use a dedicated integration user with access to every project you intend to select.

Asana PATs do not refresh automatically. Rotate by creating a replacement token, updating the connector, verifying a sync, and only then revoking the old token; removing the integration user immediately invalidates its token.
Pick the projects to sync after connecting. Tasks, subtasks, projects and comment stories become searchable; system-generated activity stories are skipped. The connector only reads Asana.

HydraDB uses Asana's privacy_setting to capture each selected project's read audience: public_to_workspace includes active, non-guest workspace members plus explicit project memberships; private includes explicit project memberships; deprecated private_to_team includes the project team's users plus explicit project memberships. Memberships can grant admins, editors, commenters, viewers or teams. If project attribution is missing, Asana omits or returns an unknown privacy setting, hides a member email, or a permission read is incomplete, HydraDB refuses a partial ACL and shows a resource-level warning under the current fail-open policy; the content remains workspace-readable unless a customer resource rule governs it. Use a dedicated integration user's personal access token that can read the selected project, its memberships, and member email addresses.

Asana quotas are per token (150 requests/minute on free domains and 1,500 on paid domains). Large comment/subtask histories fan out per task, so a dedicated token also keeps this connector from sharing quota with unrelated automations.

providers.name: Monday.com
setup_guide: Paste a Monday personal API token from Profile → Developers → My Access Tokens, or an OAuth token whose app has boards:read. A personal token inherits the user's board visibility; private boards the user cannot open will not appear in the picker.

A Monday personal token does not use an OAuth refresh flow. Rotate it by updating and validating the connector before revoking the prior token; OAuth installations must keep their provider refresh flow active.

Pick boards after connecting. Each active item becomes a searchable task containing its name and rendered column values, with board-relation columns represented as graph links. Archived/deleted items are not enumerable through Monday's board items_page API and can remain indexed until a full resync.

When Monday permission capture is disabled, selected board content is readable by everyone in the workspace with a persistent warning unless you set a resource access rule. Ask your administrator to enable Monday permission capture before relying on board restrictions.

When capture is enabled, board readers are captured from owners, subscribers, and subscribed teams. Main/public boards follow account membership; public boards in closed workspaces follow workspace membership. The token must read boards, users, teams, and workspaces (boards:read, users:read, teams:read, workspaces:read).

If a guest, team member, or workspace reader cannot be resolved to a complete user/email roster, resource ACL capture fails open with a persistent warning rather than storing a partial allow-list. Do not interpret board permissions as read access; those values govern editing.

Monday enforces GraphQL complexity budgets and daily API call limits that vary by token and account plan. The connector paginates and retries rate limits, but very large boards can require a longer sync interval.

providers.name: ClickUp
setup_guide: Create a personal API token under avatar → Settings → Apps → API Token. ClickUp personal tokens have no scope picker and inherit the user; use a dedicated account that can open every Workspace you intend to select.

ClickUp personal tokens have no refresh flow. Rotate by generating a replacement, updating the connector, verifying discovery and sync, and then revoking the old token; an OAuth installation must use ClickUp's refresh-token lifecycle instead.

Pick Workspaces after connecting. Tasks and subtasks are indexed with descriptions, status, assignees, priority, tags and list/folder context. Task comments are indexed as first-class comment documents with human author and parent-task context. ClickUp limits personal and OAuth tokens per Workspace plan, starting at 100 requests/minute on Free, Unlimited and Business.

HydraDB does not currently reproduce ClickUp guest or private Space/List/Task visibility. Synced tasks and comments are tenant-wide under the current fail-open policy, carry a persistent rbac_warning, and can be restricted with a HydraDB resource ACL for the selected Workspace.

providers.name: Airtable
setup_guide: Create an Airtable Personal Access Token with data.records:read and schema.bases:read, then grant that token access to every base you want to select. Correct scopes alone do not grant base access. Legacy API keys are retired.

Airtable Personal Access Tokens have no refresh flow. Rotate by creating a replacement with the same scopes and base grants, updating the connector, validating discovery and sync, and then revoking the old token.

Pick bases after connecting. Every table record becomes a custom searchable object; record-link fields become graph links, attachment filenames remain in record text, and supported attachment file contents are downloaded through short-lived claim-check pointers and indexed. Oversized or unsupported files remain metadata-only without blocking the record.
HydraDB does not currently import Airtable base/workspace collaborators as ACLs. Synced records are tenant-wide unless you configure a HydraDB resource ACL for the selected base.

Airtable has no reliable modified timestamp in record payloads, so the connector uses LAST_MODIFIED_TIME() server-side windows. Formula fields that depend on external state can change without a record modification event and may require a full resync.

providers.name: SharePoint
setup_guide: Register a Microsoft Entra app for app-only client credentials. Copy the Directory (tenant) ID, Application (client) ID, and a client-secret Value into tenant, client_id, and client_secret; the Secret ID is not the secret value.

Grant Microsoft Graph APPLICATION permissions Sites.Read.All and Files.Read.All, then grant tenant-wide admin consent. Sites.Read.All is required for site discovery, document libraries, and site pages; Files.Read.All is required for drive delta metadata and file-content download. Delegated permissions do not satisfy this connector.

Pick the SharePoint sites to sync. Site pages and document-library files become searchable with human site, library, path, author, and MIME metadata; IDs remain provenance and stable identity rather than reader-facing labels.

Lists on a selected site are indexed too: every row of every visible list becomes one document holding its column values under their display names. Document libraries, hidden lists and SharePoint's own system lists are skipped, and list row attachments are not downloaded.

Native SharePoint item and site permissions are not yet reproduced. Content stays tenant-public under the current fail-open policy and every source carries rbac_warning; configure a customer resource ACL for sites that must be restricted.

File changes use Graph drive delta and page changes use lastModifiedDateTime windows. Provider deletion signals are not fully converged into hard index deletion yet; this documented current limitation does not block initial or incremental ingestion.

providers.name: Intercom
setup_guide: Use an Intercom private-app access token or OAuth token with Read conversations, Read and list users and companies, Read admins, Read and List articles, and Read tickets. The connector only reads.

Rotate a private-app token by replacing the connector secret and validating a sync before revoking the old token. OAuth installations must preserve refresh tokens and reauthorize if requested scopes or teammate visibility change.

Use the token of a teammate set to All conversations. Since July 2026, an OAuth token can read only conversations visible to the teammate who authorized it. Regenerate the token after changing that setting, or the index silently narrows.

Private teammate notes are excluded by default. When acl_supported is enabled for Intercom, each assigned conversation, conversation part and ticket is readable by its assignee and the members of its assigned team. Intercom's API does not expose which teammates can see all conversations, so this is a lower bound: such a teammate who is not the assignee or on the team is denied, never over-granted.

Unassigned conversations and tickets carry no ACL of their own and follow their resource. The workspace resource is public unless you set a HydraDB resource ACL on it. Help Center articles are unrestricted. An assignee or team that cannot be resolved makes no claim and carries an rbac_warning: the object then follows its resource, which is public for the workspace resource.

Intercom applies app/workspace rate limits and paginated-search limits that can vary by endpoint and plan. The connector honors 429 backoff; high-volume workspaces should avoid overlapping full syncs with other bulk exports.

providers.name: Freshdesk
setup_guide: Copy an agent API key from Freshdesk Profile settings and enter only the helpdesk subdomain: for acme.freshdesk.com, enter acme. The key has no scope picker and reads according to that agent's Global, Group or Restricted ticket scope.

Freshdesk API keys do not refresh automatically and are tied to the agent. Rotate by resetting or replacing the key, updating the connector, and validating a sync before disabling the prior agent credential.

Tickets and public replies become searchable and link back to the agent portal. Private agent notes are off by default because Freshdesk's per-agent visibility is not yet reproduced in HydraDB; when explicitly enabled they are indexed tenant-wide with an RBAC warning, so enable include_private_notes only when every tenant member may read them.
Freshdesk rate limits are account-wide and plan-dependent. The connector honors Retry-After on 429 responses; other apps in the same helpdesk consume the same quota.

providers.name: Discord
setup_guide: Create a Discord application and bot in the Developer Portal, reset/copy the bot token, and invite it to each server with OAuth2 scope bot. Grant View Channels and Read Message History on every selected channel; the connector is read-only and never sends messages.

Enable Message Content Intent under Developer Portal → Bot → Privileged Gateway Intents. The connector verifies the application flag and refuses to sync when it is absent instead of silently indexing empty content fields.

Pick the Discord servers to sync. Every readable message in their text and announcement channels, active threads, public archived threads, and joined private archived threads becomes a message source. User, role and channel mentions are rewritten to human display names; attachments contribute filenames but their bytes are not downloaded.

Discord bot tokens have no granular API scope picker and do not expire automatically. Rotate a leaked token in the Developer Portal. Discord enforces rate-limit buckets and the connector honors Retry-After before retrying.

Discord exposes no guild-member email addresses, so provider roles and channel overwrites cannot be mapped safely to HydraDB login emails. Under the current fail-open RBAC policy Discord sources are tenant-public with a persistent warning unless a customer HydraDB resource ACL is configured.

The REST history API exposes existing messages and edits but not deletion events. A deleted Discord message can remain indexed until the connector is rebuilt from a fresh snapshot; real-time deletion capture requires the Discord Gateway and is intentionally not claimed by this pull connector.

providers.name: Microsoft Teams & Outlook
setup_guide: Connect with an Azure AD app registration (app-only, client credentials): in the Azure portal open Microsoft Entra ID → App registrations → New registration (any name, no redirect URI). Copy the Directory (tenant) ID as tenant and the Application (client) ID as client_id, then under Certificates & secrets create a client secret and paste its Value (shown once) as client_secret.

Under API permissions → Add a permission → Microsoft Graph → Application permissions (not Delegated) add Team.ReadBasic.All, Channel.ReadBasic.All, ChannelMessage.Read.All, TeamMember.Read.All and ChannelMember.Read.All for Teams channels, User.ReadBasic.All plus Mail.Read for Outlook, and Chat.Read.All to offer people's Teams chats, then click Grant admin consent (a Global or Application Administrator). The connect step reads the token's roles and names any permission that is missing; a family whose permissions are absent simply does not appear in the picker.

Reading channel and chat messages with application permissions is a Microsoft Teams protected API: after consent, submit https://aka.ms/teamsgraph/requestaccess with the Application (client) ID and tenant ID (Microsoft usually answers within a week). Until it is approved every Teams sync fails with 403 even though the permission shows as granted; the picker and Outlook work regardless.

Pick the teams, the mailboxes and the people whose Teams chats to sync in the resource-selection step. A team syncs its standard channels (root posts and replies each become a message document, replies linked to their root); a mailbox syncs every message received in the history window outside Drafts, Junk Email, Deleted Items, Outbox and Conversation History, with text bodies and attachment names; a chat user syncs the 1:1, group and meeting chats they take part in. Chats are opted in per person on purpose: they are the most private surface Graph exposes.

Every message carries who may see it in Microsoft 365: the team's members for a standard channel, the channel's members (plus the teams it is shared with) for a private or shared channel, the participants for a chat, and the mailbox owner for mail. With acl_supported on for the provider, permission-aware search shows each message only to those people. A complete roster is authoritative; when Microsoft omits, truncates or refuses a roster, the message remains tenant-public under the current fail-open policy and carries a persistent rbac_warning instead of applying a partial allow-list.

Mail.Read grants the app every mailbox in the tenant. To limit it to the mailboxes you select, create an Exchange application access policy (New-ApplicationAccessPolicy -AppId <client_id> -PolicyScopeGroupId <group> -AccessRight RestrictAccess); a selected mailbox outside the policy fails the sync with a message naming the policy rather than syncing silently empty. Leave Mail.Read out entirely for a Teams-only connector.
Private and shared channels are skipped by default (Teams shows them only to their members); set include_private_channels to true to index them, restricted to their members.

Each sync reads only what changed: Graph orders a channel's posts by the last activity of the whole thread, so an old post that gets a new reply is picked up, and mail is filtered server-side on lastModifiedDateTime. Edits re-index the message. A message deleted in Teams, and mail moved to Deleted Items or Junk Email after it was indexed, is replaced by a hidden stub on the next sync; mail purged from Deleted Items leaves no trace until a full re-sync.
Rotate the client secret before it expires (Azure defaults to 6-24 months): an expired secret stops every sync with a message naming the fix. Pasting a new secret value re-enables the connector.

providers.name: Outlook
setup_guide: Connect with an Azure AD app registration (app-only, client credentials): in the Azure portal open Microsoft Entra ID → App registrations → New registration (any name, no redirect URI). Copy the Directory (tenant) ID as tenant and the Application (client) ID as client_id, then under Certificates & secrets create a client secret and paste its Value (shown once) as client_secret.

Under API permissions → Add a permission → Microsoft Graph → Application permissions (not Delegated) add User.ReadBasic.All and Mail.Read, then click Grant admin consent (a Global or Application Administrator). The connect step fails with a message naming them when either is missing.

Pick the mailboxes to sync in the resource-selection step. A mailbox syncs every message received in the history window outside Drafts, Junk Email, Deleted Items, Outbox and Conversation History, with text bodies and attachment names.

Every email carries who may see it in Microsoft 365: the mailbox owner. With acl_supported on for the provider, permission-aware search shows each email only to that person; when the owner cannot be resolved the email remains tenant-public under the current fail-open policy and carries a persistent rbac_warning.

Mail.Read grants the app every mailbox in the tenant. To limit it to the mailboxes you select, create an Exchange application access policy (New-ApplicationAccessPolicy -AppId <client_id> -PolicyScopeGroupId <group> -AccessRight RestrictAccess); a selected mailbox outside the policy fails the sync with a message naming the policy rather than syncing silently empty.

Each sync reads only what changed: mail is filtered server-side on lastModifiedDateTime. Mail moved to Deleted Items or Junk Email after it was indexed is replaced by a hidden stub on the next sync; mail purged from Deleted Items leaves no trace until a full re-sync.
Rotate the client secret before it expires (Azure defaults to 6-24 months): an expired secret stops every sync with a message naming the fix. Pasting a new secret value re-enables the connector.

providers.name: BigQuery
setup_guide: Connect with a service-account key: paste the downloaded key file as credentials_json (grant the account the BigQuery Data Viewer and BigQuery Job User roles). client_email + private_key, or client_id + client_secret + refresh_token, also work.
Pick which tables to sync in the resource-selection step; each table's rows become searchable documents.

Replication is configured PER TABLE, alongside the selection: pass table_configs on POST /connectors/{id}/configure — the same request that selects the tables — with exactly one mode per table. The dashboard collects this on the table-selection screen.

Tables with a timestamp column that changes on every insert/update (updated_at, modified_ts, …): make it the sync cursor — table_configs: [{"table": "dataset.table", "replication_key": "updated_at"}] — and each sync reads only new and changed rows.
Append-only tables with no such column: use {"table": "dataset.table", "change_history": "appends"}. New rows stream from BigQuery's own change log — no schema change, no setup.

Tables that also receive UPDATEs but have no cursor column: use {"table": "dataset.table", "change_history": "changes"} instead, and run this once in BigQuery (no schema change, does not touch your data): ALTER TABLE dataset.table SET OPTIONS(enable_change_history=true).

Change-history backfill never blocks live syncing: changes are captured from the moment you connect, while existing rows backfill in the background in bounded slices per sync cycle. On a very large table the full backfill can take many cycles — expect it to be slow. To skip it, add "snapshot": "none" to that table's table_configs entry (only rows that change after connecting are indexed), or "snapshot": 10000 to cap the backfill at that many rows.

Fleet-wide fallbacks (optional, credential fields): a top-level "replication_key" applies that cursor to every synced table that has the column; "change_history" ("appends" | "changes") covers tables that still have no cursor. Per-table table_configs override both.

A table with no cursor and no change_history re-reads in full every sync cycle — fine for small reference tables, expensive for large ones. The dashboard requires a mode per table; API/SDK consumers should always send table_configs (or the fleet-wide fields).

providers.name: Gong
setup_guide: Connect with a Gong API key pair: in Gong's Admin center open Settings → Ecosystem → API → API keys → Get API key. Only a Gong technical administrator can create one. Copy the Access Key and the Access Key Secret (the secret is shown once) and pass them as access_key and access_key_secret.

When creating the key, leave the TTL empty: a key minted with an expiry stops the connector on that date and every sync after it fails with 401 until a new key is pasted. Leave Trusted IPs empty too, unless you add HydraDB's egress addresses; a list that excludes them fails every request with 403.

The same page shows your company's API base URL. If it is not https://api.gong.io (Gong assigns some companies their own host, e.g. https://us-12345.api.gong.io), pass it as api_base_url; only *.api.gong.io hosts are accepted.

Gong API keys are company-wide and have no scope picker, so there is nothing to under- or over-grant. The connector reads calls (metadata, CRM context, AI brief, outline, highlights, key points, outcome, public comments, transcript), users, workspaces, the call library and coaching scorecards; it never writes to Gong and never downloads media.

Pick the Gong workspaces to sync in the resource-selection step; most companies have one. Each recorded call becomes one document whose body is the transcript plus Gong's summary content; each completed coaching scorecard review becomes a document linked to its call; each call filed in a public library folder becomes a document carrying the curator's note.

Calls Gong marks private, and coaching reviews whose visibility is not PUBLIC, are skipped by default (Gong shows them only to their owner, participants or managers). Set include_private_calls to true to index them as well.

Gong publishes no modified-since filter and finishes transcripts, briefs and comments after the call itself appears, so every sync re-reads the last transcript_settle_hours (default 24) of calls and re-indexes the ones whose content changed. Raise it to catch later comments, lower it (or 0) to save requests on a very high-volume account: Gong allows 10,000 API calls per company per day, shared with every other integration you run. Because of that cap, a Gong connector syncs at most every 30 minutes (the default is hourly).

Not synced, because Gong's API does not expose them: emails and digital interactions, Gong Engage flows and tasks, forecasts, and deleted calls (a call removed in Gong stays indexed until the connector is re-synced from scratch).

providers.name: Guru
setup_guide: Connect with a Guru API token: in Guru open Manage → Apps & Integrations → API Access and click Generate User Token (Admins, and roles with the Manage Apps & Integrations permission, can generate one, including on behalf of another user). A user token pairs the Guru username, usually the email, with the token (pass them as email and api_token) and reads exactly what that user can read; there is no scope picker. A collection token pairs the collection ID with the token (pass them as collection_id and api_token) and is read-only, scoped to that one collection; the connector then offers only that collection. Set exactly one of email or collection_id.

Pick the collections to sync in the resource-selection step; each card becomes one searchable document carrying its collection, folders, tags, verification state, verifiers, owner and comment count. Comment threads and replies are separate searchable comment documents linked to their card with comment_on and to their parent thread with reply_to, not embedded into the card. Each sync picks up cards edited, re-verified or commented on since the last one.

With permission-aware search on, each collection is restricted to the members of the Guru groups that can open it. Reading that needs the user token of a Guru Admin or of the collection's owner. With a collection token, or a member's token Guru refuses, the collection stays readable by everyone in this workspace and the connector shows a warning naming the token to use, until you reconnect with one or set an access rule on the resource.

Restricted (PRIVATE) cards are skipped by default: Guru shows them only to their author and the people they are shared with. Set include_private_cards to index them too; each is then indexed with exactly that audience (author and live collaborators, groups expanded to their members), enforced while permission-aware search is on. A card whose audience cannot be read completely is still indexed, with its collection's access.

providers.name: SurveyMonkey
setup_guide: Use a SurveyMonkey app access token with View Surveys (surveys_read) and View Response Details (responses_read_detail). A draft app token expires after 90 days unless the app is deployed.
Before a draft token expires, replace it in the connector and validate discovery and sync; deployed OAuth apps must retain their refresh-token flow and reauthorize when scopes change.

Pick surveys after connecting. The full questionnaire and human-readable response answers are indexed; collectors and contacts are not. Basic accounts expose at most 25 detailed responses per survey through the API, while paid plans allow the complete response history.
HydraDB does not currently import SurveyMonkey team sharing as ACLs. Survey questions and responses are tenant-wide unless you configure a HydraDB resource ACL for the selected survey.

providers.name: Okta
setup_guide: Create an API token: Okta admin console → Security → API → Tokens → Create Token. There is no scope picker and no role selector on that dialog — the token silently inherits the role of whoever creates it.

That inheritance is the thing to get right. To get a least-privilege token you must be signed in AS a Read-only Administrator when you mint it; minting as a Super Admin gives you a Super Admin token with nothing in the UI saying so. Check the Role column in the token list afterwards to confirm what you actually created.

The create form has a required dropdown, "API calls made with this token must originate from". Leaving it unset fails with only "We found some errors" and no indication of which field. Choose Any IP unless you have defined an Okta network zone covering HydraDB's egress addresses.

Set the org URL to your own org host, keeping the /api/v1/ path and the trailing slash: https://<org>.okta.com/api/v1/ . The -admin host answers the API too, so either hostname works — the path and trailing slash are the part that matters.

Two expiry traps. The token is bound to its creating user, so deactivating that person breaks the sync with 403s. And Okta expires a token after 30 days of no use, while the admin session itself is short-lived — so mint it and paste it in one sitting.

Nothing is picked after connecting: Okta syncs the whole org. Users, groups, applications and system log events are indexed, with group membership, app assignments and MFA enrolment folded into the user, group and application records.

providers.name: LaunchDarkly
setup_guide: Create the token in LaunchDarkly under Account settings → Authorization → Access tokens → Create token. LaunchDarkly has no scope checkboxes: a token carries a ROLE, and the role is the whole decision.

Set Role to Reader, which is the default. Reader is all this connector needs — verified against the API, every endpoint it calls answers 200 with a read-only token. Writer or Admin add only write access, so they buy you nothing and let a leaked token turn your flags on and off.

Tick "This is a service token". A personal token inherits the role of whoever minted it and stops working the moment that person is deactivated, which is the most common way this connection breaks. The token is shown once — copy it before closing the dialog.
After connecting, pick the projects to sync. Everything project-scoped follows that choice: the project's flags, its environments, and its segments.

Some data is account-wide and is always synced, whatever you pick: the audit log, account members and teams. Members and teams are what let a flag's maintainer resolve to a person or a group rather than a raw id.

Flags are indexed with their real targeting, per environment — on/off state, the default variation or percentage rollout, individual targets, prerequisite flags and each rule, including which segment a rule matches. Segments are indexed alongside, so "who is this flag on for" is answerable end to end.

Two things are deliberately never indexed. An environment's SDK key and mobile key are dropped before they leave the tap, because they are live credentials for your own environment. So are a member's MFA state and whether they have a password.

A brand-new LaunchDarkly organization has one empty default project and no flags, so a correctly configured connector on a new org indexes almost nothing. That is the org being empty, not the token being wrong.

With permission-aware search on, each project is restricted to the members who can view it in LaunchDarkly: their base role, custom roles (preset roles included), team roles and permission grants are evaluated the way LaunchDarkly does. Flags, segments and environments follow their project, and so does each audit log entry about one project; members, teams and account-level audit entries are not restricted. Invited members who have not joined yet are not included. The token's role must read projects, members, teams and custom roles (the built-in Reader can). A role this evaluation cannot read exactly makes every project readable by everyone in your workspace, with a warning on the connector naming it.

providers.name: attio
setup_guide: Connect with a workspace API key: Attio workspace settings → Developers → API keys. The key is static and does not expire, so this connection never needs reconnecting.

Grant the key the read scopes for records, objects, lists, list entries, notes, tasks, comments and users. A key missing a scope fails with a 403 that names it — granting them all up front is faster than finding out one at a time.

Pass the key as access_token. Objects (people, companies, deals, custom ones) and lists are picked in the resource-selection step after connecting — leaving the objects/lists credential fields empty is the normal path.

With permission-aware search on, a private list's entries are restricted to the workspace's admins and the members the list is shared with; a list shared with the whole workspace, and every record, note, task, comment and meeting, is readable by everyone in your workspace. Attio's API does not expose team grants, so a member who reaches a list only through a team does not see it here. The key needs the List Configuration: Read and User Management: Read scopes; without them the list is readable by everyone, with a warning, until you reconnect.

providers.name: twitter
setup_guide: You bring your own X developer app: X bills API reads per record to the app owner ($0.005/post, $0.010/user read), so the connector never fronts a shared app.

Posts only (recommended): in the X developer portal open Projects & Apps → your app, and complete 'User authentication settings' once if it is empty — that is what creates the app's OAuth 2.0 client. Then on the Keys and tokens page, in the 'OAuth 2.0 Client ID and Client Secret' section, copy the Client ID and Generate the Client Secret (X shows it only once) — pass them as client_id and client_secret. Do NOT use the API Key and API Key Secret listed above them: those are OAuth 1.0a keys and will not work. The connector mints its own app-only token from them on every sync; nothing expires, so this connection never needs reconnecting. Add the handles to follow (any public account).

Direct messages additionally need an OAuth2 user-context token — X serves DMs to no other auth scheme. First set the app's permissions to 'Read and write and Direct message' (User authentication settings): that setting is what allows the dm.read scope to be granted at all, and changing it later invalidates tokens already issued. Set the app type to the confidential-client option (Web App, Automated App or Bot) so the app has a client secret — both the app-only mint and token refresh require one.

Then, for your own account, generate the token pair straight from the portal: the Keys and tokens page has an OAuth 2.0 token generator — pick the scopes (dm.read tweet.read users.read offline.access) and it returns the access token and refresh token together. offline.access is the scope that produces the refresh token. To read a DIFFERENT account's inbox, that account must instead complete the authorization-code flow against your app once, since the portal only issues tokens for the logged-in account.

Pass the resulting tokens as access_token AND refresh_token, alongside client_id and client_secret. The access token expires after ~2 hours; the refresh token is what lets the platform renew it indefinitely. A DM connector without refresh_token stops syncing when the access token expires.
DM ingest is an explicit opt-in: even with a user token, the inbox appears as its own resource in the selection step and is never synced unless selected.

History limits are X's, not ours: the DM API serves only the most recent 30 days of events, so a DM backfill reaches back at most 30 days (the dashboard caps the history window accordingly); post timelines reach roughly the 3,200 most recent posts per account.

Spend guards: max_posts_per_account_per_sync (default 500) and max_dms_per_sync (default 1000) cap billed reads per sync and log a warning when hit; sync_profiles is off by default because a user read costs double a post read.

providers.name: Supabase
providers.summary: Selected table row changes arrive through database webhooks. There is no history backfill.
setup_guide: List the tables you want indexed, one per line, as schema.table, for example public.customers. Always include the schema.
In your Supabase project, install the Database Webhooks integration if it is not already installed.
Establish the connection in the HydraDB dashboard, then select the tables you want to sync.
Run the SQL command generated by the dashboard in the Supabase SQL editor to add a trigger for each table. Replace the API key placeholder with your HydraDB API key.
Only changes made after connecting are reflected. Existing rows are sent when they are updated; there is no historical backfill.
